title: Dial-A-Priority Negotiator — SLA-aware adaptive phase splitting for prefill/decode
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Our current prefill/decode pipeline uses static phase-splitting heuristics (fixed prefill chunk sizes and coarse tenant weights) that cause either wasted kernel work (over-splitting) or long queues and SLA misses (under-splitting) for mixed workloads. We need a lightweight controller that negotiates per-request priority against system load and kernel profiles so we can dynamically choose phase splits, hedging, and demotion without blowing up scheduling complexity.

Goal: Design and implement a 'Dial-A-Priority' negotiator that: (1) accepts a per-request SLA/utility hint (latency target, cost sensitivity, or hybrid), (2) computes an adaptive phase split plan (initial prefill size, follow-on decode batching strategy, hedging thresholds), and (3) produces kernel-selection hints for the runtime (e.g., quantized fastpath vs precision path) while respecting tenant fairness budgets. The controller should be explainable (traceable decisions), cheap to compute, and pluggable into the existing prefill/decode arbitration layer.

Proposed approach:
- Request-level utility model: map latency/cost hint into a numeric utility score and deadline budget. Default mapping profiles: latency-first, balanced, economical.
- Adaptive phase-splitting: compute an initial prefill fraction f in [0.05, 0.6] based on request utility and current queue latency percentiles. Lower f for economical workloads, higher f for latency-sensitive. Use bounded exponential smoothing to avoid oscillation.
- Kernel hinting: expose a short hint set to the runtime: {fastpath_quant, fastpath_fused_attn, precise_fp16}. Negotiator prefers fastpath when utility prioritizes latency and model/profile supports it.
- Fairness & tenant budgets: account for tenant credits (soft quotas) so negotiator will probabilistically demote low-credit tenants under sustained congestion. Demotions are transparent in traces.
- Hedging and fallbacks: if predicted time-to-first-token exceeds latency budget, issue an opportunistic hedged slice (speculative decode) to a lower-fidelity kernel. Limit hedges per-tenant to avoid cost explosion.
- Attention-sparsity signal: use upstream attention-density estimator (from tracing stats) to adjust phase granularity: high sparsity -> larger prefill chunks (more efficient), dense attention -> smaller chunks to reduce kernel tail.
- Safety & cost controls: soft global knobs to cap total hedges and kernel-swap frequency; safety thresholds for privacy workloads (no hedging for certain governance labels).

Implementation plan:
1) Define negotiator API and hint envelope (RFC doc + proto): small fixed-size JSON for speed. (Owner: Marco)
2) Implement utility mapper + phase-split heuristic in Rust service layer (low CPU budget). Start with rule-based mapper, add learned components later. (Owner: Aisha)
3) Runtime integration: add kernel-hint consumer and hedging actuator in prefill/decode arbiter. Minimal back-and-forth: negotiator returns plan synchronously when request is admitted. (Owner: Runtime team pair)
4) Telemetry & tracing: add `negotiator.decisions` span, record chosen f, kernel_hint, estimated_latency, and final outcome. Build dashboard for tuning.
5) Safety QA: synthetic load tests that vary utility mixes, attention sparsity, and tenant credit states. Validate fairness via percentile comparison across tenant cohorts.

Trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs latency: a heavy ML policy would learn better trade-offs but risks added inference latency. We prefer a deterministic rule engine + small adaptive smoothing initially.
- Cost visibility: hedges reduce tail latency but increase token cost. Expose per-tenant cost delta and allow customers to opt-out.
- Kernel hints are advisory, not binding — runtime may override for compatibility. This reduces guarantee but keeps integration simpler.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end path with negotiator producing plans and runtime honoring kernel hints in at least 80% of decisions under normal load.
- Tail (P99) latency improvement of at least 15% for latency-first workloads under mixed load compared to baseline.
- No more than 10% increase in average token cost for hedged workload profiles across tests.
- Fairness: under congestion, top-50% tenants maintain at least 90% of baseline success rate while lower-credit tenants see controlled demotion documented in traces.
